diagnosis.what_is_wrong: No kernel evidence establishes a fault causing the coding task to run slowly. Activity varies sharply, including a short python3 CPU burst, but measured CPU use stays below one core on average in that burst and the sampled runnable-to-running delays are only 12–19 microseconds; this supports normal workload variation rather than demonstrated CPU contention or another diagnosed bottleneck.
diagnosis.evidence: Compared the trace span from ctf_timespan (03:24:07.500–03:24:26.200) with the per-interval event rates and summed sched_stat_runtime values computed from the full trace. Rates collapse after 03:24:08.2 and later vary, but the clearest CPU burst, 03:24:18.500–03:24:22.500, totals 3.181 CPU-seconds over four seconds (0.795 cores), of which python3 uses 2.929 CPU-seconds. In sampled raw scheduler records, wakeup-to-switch delays are at most 0.019 ms. Sampled network transmissions succeeded; the available block records do not provide request completion latency, and reclaim/OOM and block request issue/complete events were unavailable, so those mechanisms cannot be fully assessed. Process-lifetime and sampled exit/fork/exec records did not show a service crash/respawn; the apparent tail exits were shell-command activity.
diagnosis.window_evidence: There is no supported incident boundary: the pronounced event-rate fall begins around 03:24:08.3, activity partially rebounds around 03:24:15.5, and the runtime-only python3 burst occurs around 03:24:18.5–22.5 before dropping. None is paired with measured scheduler delay or another decisive fault signature, so assigning any of these as the incident window would overstate the evidence.
